approaches.fromDirection: east, up the escarpment from the Hist court on the gorge floor
approaches.notes: The only approach for a cart. The climb costs 40 m and pays at the gate with the view back down onto the crown of the Hist.
approaches.sequence: From the Hist court on the gorge floor the conduit-head pillar reads on the lip 40 m above, with the amber line running down the face to the tree; the first traverse turns away and the face hides it; the second bend brings the gate wall across the road with the pillar beside it; through the gate the yard opens and the great stair stands ahead; at its head the statue wall.
approaches.wayfinding: Follow the amber conduit up the face; it leads to the gate. Inside the gate the road runs straight to the foot of the great stair.

approaches.notes: The raiders' way in and the taken labourers' only way out that avoids the gate. It arrives at the pens, not the works, so a player meets the taken before the tribe.
approaches.sequence: From the shoulder at 240 m the watch column reads first, a thin stone thing against the void of the gorge with the grey crown of the Hist behind it; the ridge track drops behind the western rise and loses it; the frontage dais and the pen fence appear at the shelf head; then the shelf gate comes across the track, 15 m of timber with a walkway over the opening; through it the terrace runs east past the great stair head to the column at the lip.
approaches.wayfinding: Follow the ridge track along the shoulder to the dais at the shelf head; the gate beyond it is the entrance. The terrace inside runs to the great stair and the column.

causalModel.founding: The Xit-Xaht went on cutting stone after the Duskfall told every tribe to stop, on the order of a Hist they had bound with sap.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: Tsono-Xuhil has not woken. The Amber Plasm seep has resumed and the conduits carry it up the escarpment into the works. The courses have started rising again.
causalModel.pressures: Labour. Every course needs hands the tribe does not have, so the pens fill from the neighbouring villages; the shelf is also too small for what the shaper has drawn.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: A firm rock shelf at the end of an upland ridge, 68 m by 42 m of buildable ground with the block face in its own southern lip. A headwater stream along that lip serves for mortar and slaking. The east side falls away in a 55 m escarpment that no neighbour climbs uninvited.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: The conduits were cut, or another tribe accepted the invitation to help.

combatSpaces.why: The stone rite of LV28 is put to a visitor before the statue wall; refusing it flips the place hostile and the shaper's watch comes down the terrace to this court.
The hostility flip closes the gate; the watch fights on the road head with the escarpment behind the defender and the gate wall in front.
A night fight in the pens when the labourer who remembers is taken to be held harder (LV28), between the shells and against the fence.
The carver's quarrel with the overseers in LV29 comes to blows among the scaffolds; the first fight after the hostility flip is here, inside the gate.

districts.notes: The upper step, 205-209 m. Mud shells, an oven and racks for the taken labourers, who are not Xit-Xaht and are not permitted stone.

why.microGeography: The upper of the three steps, 14 m deep and flat at about 207 m, with the ridge rising behind it and a 2 m riser held by the north course in front.
why.playerPurpose: The place where a player meets the taken and hears what the tribe does not say; three small interiors and the LV28 confidences.
why.what: The pens: three mud shells, an oven and a rack for the taken labourers, fenced on the uphill and east sides.
why.whyHere: The Xit-Xaht raid their neighbours for labour; the taken are kept apart from the tribe, above the works and in the material of the province rather than in stone.
why.whyNeighbours: The works terrace lies below, so the overseers look straight down into the pens; the pens stair climbs from the terrace and nothing else does, so the pens are met after the gate and the court, not before them.

districts.notes: The lower step and the stream lip, 196-203 m. Block face, hoist, scaffolds, gate and cart. The stockade scaffold family is placed per its own snap logic.

why.microGeography: The lowest step, 12 m deep at about 200 m, with the headwater stream 3 to 8 m below its southern lip.
why.playerPurpose: The first node inside the gate, cluttered and loud: the carver, the walkway keeper and the yard fight.
why.what: The staging yard: the block face, the hoist, the scaffolds, the cart and the gate.
why.whyHere: The shelf's own rock is the quarry and the stream at the lip slakes the lime; the yard is where the stone is cut and hauled before it climbs.
why.whyNeighbours: The gate closes its east end and the great stair leaves its west; everything in it moves between those two points.

districts.notes: The middle step, 198-206 m. The half-built quarter. The IGS Ayleid pieces and the Here There Be Monsters xanmeer pieces stand in separate parcels and never abut. Declared a surveyed line (97 C2/C8): a xanmeer is laid on a 90-degree grid (module 97 Part F, argonian-stone); the two risers are built straight walls; every course and stair is squared to them, so the district's pieces share the cardinal bearing by design.

why.microGeography: The middle step, 17 m deep, falling from 206 m at the pens riser to 200 m at the yard riser; every course runs along a riser and both stairs run on the fall line.
why.playerPurpose: The centre node: the statue wall, the interior entrance, the shaper's station, the rite of LV28 and the argument of LV29.
why.what: The works: the half-built stone quarter, its courses, statue wall, stair-throat, kiln, watch column and the conduit head.
why.whyHere: The stone heresy of the Xit-Xaht made visible: courses rising three centuries late, on the one shelf of the ridge wide enough to carry them.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the pens above and the yard below, so the labour comes down to it and the stone comes up to it; the conduit enters it at the lip.

landmarks.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/ruins/xanmeer/pillar02
landmarks.notes: Where the amber run crests the escarpment lip and turns into the works. The parcel parcel.mazzatun.conduit-pillar places the piece; this landmark names the point.

why.microGeography: On the lip at 198 m with the 55 m face below.
why.playerPurpose: The first-seen object from the haul road and the LV28 encounter socket.
why.what: The point at which the amber run crests the lip: the top of the conduit-pillar.
why.whyHere: The signature feature of the record needs one readable point. That point is the moment at which the sap arrives.
why.whyNeighbours: The gate wall's outer end and the tower are beside it; the road passes beneath it.
why.whySpot: The lowest point of the lip above the road's last bend.

landmarks.notes: Tsono-Xuhil, its own catalogue record (place.dunmer-north.mazzatun-hist), 85 m east and 55 m below the shelf. Never cleared and never built over.

why.microGeography: In the channel at 148 m, its crown 30 m or more above the gorge floor and still below the shelf.
why.playerPurpose: The province-changing lore reveal of LV26 and the foot of the climb.
why.what: Tsono-Xuhil, the harmed Hist, standing in the stream on the gorge floor.
why.whyHere: The city was built around the tree and the tree was bound to build the city; the conduits start at its roots.
why.whyNeighbours: The haul road starts at its court; the conduit leaves it; the shelf looks down on it.
why.whySpot: It stands where it always stood, at the waterfall landform on which its own record was won.

networkTerminals.why: The ridge track from the rimfield reaches the shelf at its west end, where a cart can leave the shoulder without crossing the pens; the terrace carries it east past the frontage dais to the tower, so track and terrace are one line.

parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/ruins/xanmeer/pillar05
parcels.orientationWhy: Set along the conduit run, which the pillar carries over the yard road toward the throat.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 201 m on the riser between the yard and the terrace.
why.playerPurpose: The amber line overhead is the wayfinding line from the gate to the throat.
why.what: A short xanmeer pillar carrying the amber conduit over the head of the yard.
why.whyHere: The conduit has to cross the yard road above head height. The tribe carries it on the ancestors' pillars.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands 3 m south of the terrace track and 4 m inside the gate; the run continues to the throat door.
why.whySpot: Between the gate wall and the stair-throat, at the point at which the run turns from the lip toward the throat.

parcels.assetRef: htbm:here there be monsters - curse of cipactli/architecture/ruins/xanmeer/pillar02
parcels.orientationWhy: The conduit head takes the run straight off the escarpment, so the channel does not turn on the lip.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 198 m on the lip, the escarpment beneath it.
why.playerPurpose: The first-seen object from the haul road: a thin thing on the skyline with the amber running down it.
why.what: The conduit head: a xanmeer pillar of 9 m at the lip, where the amber run crests the escarpment.
why.whyHere: The sap climbs 55 m from the Hist to the works. The head is where it arrives; the signature feature of the record is made visible by this one piece.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands at the gate wall's outer end, so the road passes beneath the head before it reaches the gate.
why.whySpot: The lowest point of the lip above the road's last bend, so that the run climbs the face in one line.

parcels.orientationWhy: The eastern bay takes the lip at a right angle to the north course, running due north from the tower: the east side of the grid.

why.microGeography: Dug into the lip at about 203 m, one face over the drop.
why.playerPurpose: From the shoulder it is the long shape behind the column; from the gorge it is the parapet above the climb.
why.what: A second arched bay, the east course of the wall along the escarpment lip.
why.whyHere: The east side of the city has the drop for a wall; the course here is the tribe's parapet against the gorge.
why.whyNeighbours: It runs from the tower toward the east pen, closing the works against the lip.
why.whySpot: Along the lip north of the tower, where the shelf edge is straight.

parcels.orientationWhy: Wall course laid along the built upper riser, which runs due east-west: the arched bay is squared to the riser line.

why.microGeography: Dug into the riser at about 204 m, its back against the pens step.
why.playerPurpose: The first stone that reads as building rather than ruin; the arch frames the pens above for a player on the terrace.
why.what: An arched stone bay, the north course of the wall as far as it has risen.
why.whyHere: The Xit-Xaht build in stone against the Duskfall prohibition. The north course is the oldest of the resumed work.
why.whyNeighbours: It runs from the corner block toward the statue wall. The frontage dais stands in front of it.
why.whySpot: Along the riser between the pens and the works, so the course is also the retaining wall of the pens above it.

parcels.orientationWhy: The corner block is squared to the upper riser on the same cardinal line as the north course; the western return will leave it at a right angle.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 203 m at the corner of the step, with the riser to the pens 2 m north of it.
why.playerPurpose: The plan of the city, legible in one block: from here the walk reads which way the courses will run.
why.what: The corner block of the wall course, a quad block turning north into west.
why.whyHere: A stone building has corners. This is the one that the shaper has finished; it fixes the plan of the whole west wing.
why.whyNeighbours: It closes the north course begun by the arched bay and starts the west return of the single block; the frontage dais is 6 m to its south.
why.whySpot: The north-west corner of the middle step, against the riser to the pens, so the course above has a footing.

parcels.orientationWhy: One block dropped at the riser line and not yet squared to it: the western course is barely begun.

why.microGeography: Dug in at about 204 m on the last flat of the middle step, with the ground falling west and south of it.
why.playerPurpose: Evidence of the resumed building: a block set within the last decade on mortar that is still pale.
why.what: A single dressed block, the first of the western return of the wall course.
why.whyHere: The building has restarted and works outward from the frontage; the west return is where the newest course begins.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands 6 m west of the corner block and 8 m above the half-cut blocks in the yard from which it was carried.
why.whySpot: The west end of the middle step, where the shelf runs out into the shoulder, so the course stops where the ground does.

parcels.orientationWhy: The working floor is opened along the block face, which follows the contour of the lower lip.

why.microGeography: Dug into the lip at about 200 m, the headwater stream 3 to 8 m south of it.
why.playerPurpose: The carver's npc socket for LV29 and the place from which the sound of stone being cut carries into the swamp.
why.what: The block face: the cutting floor from which the shelf's own stone is taken.
why.whyHere: The shelf is the quarry; the city is built from the rock beneath it. The face is at the southern lip where the stream slakes the cut.
why.whyNeighbours: The hoist stands over it; the scaffolds and the half-cut blocks are up-slope of it.
why.whySpot: Against the western rise, where the shelf runs out into rock and the face can be cut back without touching the courses.

parcels.orientationWhy: The frontage dais is squared to the lower riser above the yard, its steps looking due south down the fall of the shelf.

why.microGeography: Dug into the riser between the works and the yard at about 202 m.
why.playerPurpose: The west end of the terrace track pays with the view down the yard and across the gorge to the crown of the Hist.
why.what: A stepped dais, the frontage of the half-built quarter, facing the yard below.
why.whyHere: A stone city needs a face turned to the people who feed it; the dais is where the shaper stands to address the gang.
why.whyNeighbours: Below it are the half-cut blocks and the scaffolds; behind it the corner block and the arched bay. The terrace track ends at it.
why.whySpot: The west end of the middle step above the yard, so that a speaker on the dais is seen from the whole yard.

parcels.orientationWhy: The flight is set square to the lower riser between the yard and the terrace, rising due north on the fall line.

why.microGeography: Cut into the riser between about 200 m and 204 m at the middle of the shelf.
why.playerPurpose: The visible means of ascent from the yard; the reveal of the statue wall as the head is reached.
why.what: The great stair: an open stone flight from the staging yard up to the works terrace.
why.whyHere: The processional line of the city turns from the haul road up onto the terrace here; the Xit-Xaht built the flight first, because the blocks go up it.
why.whyNeighbours: The yard road ends at its foot; the terrace track passes its head; the statue wall stands above it.
why.whySpot: At the yard's inner end where the riser is straightest, in line with the gate so that a player through the gate sees the flight ahead.

parcels.orientationWhy: Half-cut stone tipped along the cut line, parallel to the face from which it was taken.

why.microGeography: Tipped on the yard floor at about 201 m, dug into the fall of the riser.
why.playerPurpose: The evidence socket of the record: the half-cut blocks that LV29's carver reads as a stone that remembers.
why.what: A pile of half-cut blocks, dressed on one face and abandoned on the others.
why.whyHere: The building stopped for three centuries and has restarted; the blocks show both facts, old cuts and new.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the scaffolds and the hoist, on the line from the block face to the great stair.
why.whySpot: In the west of the yard below the frontage, where the carts tip.

parcels.orientationWhy: Standing in line with the yard road, shafts down where the last load was tipped.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 199 m on the yard floor beside the road.
why.playerPurpose: A prop that says a working day is in progress. It gives cover in the yard fight.
why.what: A hand cart, shafts down, beside the yard road inside the gate.
why.whyHere: Blocks and lime move on carts between the block face, the hoist and the great stair.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the road and the scaffold stair.
why.whySpot: Just inside the gate, off the road, where the carts wait for the gang.

parcels.notes: A compound gate, not a gatehouse: the Redoran piece carries no room, so the watch stands on the terrace behind it.
parcels.orientationWhy: Set to 1.3° so the gate's 7.3 m run stands square across the haul road it spans, on the line the timber gate it replaced held; the Redoran piece carries its run 2.2° off the old one in its own frame, which the yaw takes up.

why.microGeography: Dug into the lip between about 197 m and 201 m, its 7.3 m run set across the road with the rock of the tower footing closing the gap to the north.
why.playerPurpose: The threshold of Mazzatun: the road is spanned, not passed, so the player is stopped in the opening and read.
why.what: A Redoran compound gate of 7.3 m, 10.1 m to the parapet, standing across the haul road at the head of the climb. Its clear opening is 3.5 m, which passes the 3 m road under it.
why.whyHere: The taken must be kept in and the neighbours out; the gate is the point at which the escarpment can be closed.
why.whyNeighbours: The tower anchors its north side; the cart stands inside it; the conduit passes over its north end.
why.whySpot: Where the road crests the lip and the shelf is narrowest, between the tower and the stream lip.

parcels.orientationWhy: The hoist beam overhangs down the fall, out over the block face below.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 202 m on the lip of the cut, 3 m above the yard floor.
why.playerPurpose: Cover and a vertical marker at the yard's south edge; a rope and beam over the stream.
why.what: A timber hoist standing over the block face, its beam out above the cut.
why.whyHere: Blocks are lifted out of the cut and onto the carts; the hoist is how the tribe raises what it cannot carry.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the cutting floor and the half-cut blocks, clear of both. The kit has no authored joint from a hoist to a rock face or to a block pile, so the three are set as a working group.
why.whySpot: Between the cut face and the pile of half-cut blocks, so a block comes off the face, up the hoist and onto the pile in one movement.

parcels.orientationWhy: The stoke hole faces north to the yard road, so the fuel comes to it off the carts without crossing the courses; its long axis lies along the stream lip.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 202 m on the riser, its mouth uphill.
why.playerPurpose: Smoke by day and glow by night: the second beacon of the place from the gorge after the conduit head.
why.what: A lime kiln for the mortar of the courses.
why.whyHere: Stone building needs mortar and the swamp has no lime; the kiln burns shell and stream stone for it.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands west of the great stair and below the frontage, out of the yard's traffic.
why.whySpot: On the stream lip at the east end of the yard, downwind and downstream of the courses and the pens, where its smoke and lime wash go over the escarpment.

parcels.notes: Door side: the flat panel on the shell's local south face, turned by the yaw to bearing 188.
parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 69.6° so the shell's one doorway looks out at 182° onto the pen lane, the walk the overseers keep.

why.microGeography: A pad on the flat of the upper step at about 207 m, with its back 6 m from the rise to the ridge and its door 3 m from the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The first interior a player reaches off the pens stair; the labourer who has begun to remember sleeps here.
why.what: A mud shell for four or five of the taken labourers, the westernmost of the three pens.
why.whyHere: The Xit-Xaht raid their neighbours for labour and keep the taken apart from the tribe; the pens are where the taken sleep. They are built in mud because the taken are not permitted stone.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands beside the racks and the oven, the two things the taken use before the shift. Its door faces the same lane as the other two shells.
why.whySpot: The upper step is the part of the shelf from which nothing leads away: rock rises behind it and the works terrace lies below, so a pen here is watched from below and walled by the hill above.

parcels.notes: Door side: the flat panel on the shell's local south face, turned by the yaw to bearing 157.
parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 30.8°, its doorway on 143° onto the pen lane, so the second shell is entered off the same walk as the first.

why.microGeography: Dug into the middle of the step at about 207 m, 4 m above the works terrace and 4 m from the lane.
why.playerPurpose: The overseers watch this pen hardest. A shift spent inside it is how their rota is learnt.
why.what: The middle pen, a mud shell for four or five taken labourers.
why.whyHere: Three pens hold the labour that the resumed building needs; the record's taken labourers are housed here and nowhere else.
why.whyNeighbours: It sits between the first pen and the pens stair, so the gang that files down to the works each shift passes its door.
why.whySpot: The middle of the upper step, where the ground is flattest, so it is a pad and not a cut.

parcels.notes: Door side: the flat panel on the shell's local south face, turned by the yaw to bearing 270.
parcels.orientationWhy: Turned to 153.0°, its doorway on 265° onto the upper end of the pen lane, where the walk bends behind the rise.

why.microGeography: Dug into the last flat of the upper step at about 205 m, with the escarpment lip 8 m to the east.
why.playerPurpose: The bed that a visitor who takes a shift is given. It is the floor on which the taken sleep, which is the tribe's answer to what a guest is.
why.what: A mud shell for four or five of the taken labourers. It is the easternmost of the three. The tribe puts working visitors on its floor as well.
why.whyHere: The taken labourers need one place where they are not watched. The tribe has let one shell stand crosswise because the ground there falls too hard for a downhill door.
why.whyNeighbours: Its door faces the pens stair and the end of the lane, not the works; the fence returns down its east side.
why.whySpot: At the east end of the pen lane in the fence corner, the last shell before the east course, drawn far enough from the pens stair that the stair head stays clear.

parcels.orientationWhy: Mouth to the lane and out of the wind that comes over the top of the step.

why.microGeography: A pad on the flat of the step at about 207 m, 3 m from the lane.
why.playerPurpose: Labourers stand idle here, within earshot of a player.
why.what: A carapace oven at which the taken cook what they are given.
why.whyHere: The taken are fed in the pens, not at the works, so the oven is on the upper step with the shells.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the racks and the first pen, so the west end of the lane is where the taken gather before the shift.
why.whySpot: Beside the racks at the west end of the step, the end farthest from the pens stair and the works.

parcels.orientationWhy: Racks laid along the contour so that the run drains one way.

why.microGeography: A pad on the last flat of the step at about 206 m before the ground climbs west to the shoulder.
why.playerPurpose: The marker at which the pens lane ends; the first object of Mazzatun read from the ridge track below the rise.
why.what: A drying rack for the fish and the reed on which the pens live.
why.whyHere: The taken are fed on what the swamp gives, dried on the step where the wind reaches it.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands at the end of the lane beside the oven, above the ridge track.
why.whySpot: The west end of the upper step, where the lane ends and the ground climbs west to the rise, so the rack is the last thing on the lane and the first thing seen from the ridge track passing below.

parcels.orientationWhy: The flight is set on the fall line so that it climbs the riser in the shortest run.

why.microGeography: Cut into the riser between about 204 m and 206 m at the east end of the middle step.
why.playerPurpose: The visible way up to the pens from the works. It is also the way down for a labourer who runs.
why.what: A short stone flight of two metres between the works terrace and the pens.
why.whyHere: The gang goes down to the works and back every shift; the riser between the two steps needs a stair. The Xit-Xaht cut it in stone.
why.whyNeighbours: Its foot is beside the stair-throat and its head is at the end of the pens lane, so the two stairs of Mazzatun stand within 10 m of each other. One climbs to the pens and the other descends into the throat.
why.whySpot: The riser is lowest here, at the east end of the middle step, so the flight is the shortest.

parcels.orientationWhy: Scaffold bay squared to the course that it serves, so its decks run along the riser.

why.microGeography: Dug into the riser at about 202 m at the west end of the yard.
why.playerPurpose: A climbable frame from which the courses are seen at hand height.
why.what: A four-sided scaffold bay under the western courses.
why.whyHere: The courses rise from scaffolds; this bay serves the western return.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands west of the half-cut blocks and below the frontage dais.
why.whySpot: Below the corner block and the single block, at the west end of the yard.

parcels.orientationWhy: Scaffold bay squared to the block face, decks along the same riser line.

why.microGeography: Dug into the lower step at about 202 m beside the block face.
why.playerPurpose: Cover in the yard fight and a frame against the stream lip.
why.what: A four-sided scaffold bay beside the block face.
why.whyHere: The block face is worked from a frame when the cut is high.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the hoist and the cutting floor.
why.whySpot: South of the yard road, west of the cutting floor.

parcels.orientationWhy: Two-sided bay laid on the four-sided base's west face, on the base's own bearing, because that is the face on which the stockade kit joins bays. Its open sides look down the yard road.

why.microGeography: Dug into the yard floor at about 201 m where it breaks toward the riser.
why.playerPurpose: Cover in the yard and a frame under the dais.
why.what: A two-sided scaffold bay below the kiln and the frontage.
why.whyHere: The frontage dais and the kiln are served from this bay.
why.whyNeighbours: It stands between the half-cut blocks and the great stair.
why.whySpot: Joined to the four-sided base as one deck at the head of the yard, between the block pile and the great stair.

parcels.orientationWhy: The flight is set on the four-sided base's south face, which is the joint that the stockade kit's own builders use, so the stair is built into the deck that it climbs. It rises against the fall with its foot on the lower step.

why.microGeography: A pad at about 199 m on the yard floor, at the foot of the fall the stair climbs.
why.playerPurpose: The LV30 npc socket: the keeper whose route knowledge exists nowhere else.
why.what: A timber scaffold stair, the walkway keeper's post.
why.whyHere: The scaffolds are climbed by their stairs. The keeper of the walkways stands at the foot of the stair nearest the gate.
why.whyNeighbours: It is built onto the south face of the four-sided base. The two-sided bay is on that base's west face, so stair and bay are one deck. The keeper watches the gate from the foot of the flight.
why.whySpot: Against the south side of the four-sided base, the flight facing the yard so the climb is seen from the road.

parcels.notes: No room here either; the shoulder falls away on both sides of the run.
parcels.orientationWhy: Set to 134.7° so the gate's 7.3 m run stands square across the ridge track it spans. The track leaves the shelf head on 302°; the Redoran piece carries its run 77.3° off its own zero, which the yaw takes up.

why.microGeography: Dug into the shelf head between about 196 m and 199 m, its 7.3 m run set across the shoulder with the pen riser above closing the rest.
why.playerPurpose: The western threshold: the ridge track is spanned, not passed, so an arriving player is stopped and read before entering the works.
why.what: The twin of the haul gate at the west head of the shelf, the same Redoran gate across the ridge track.
why.whyHere: The Xit-Xaht close both ends of the shelf: a works built on taken labour is shut at the ridge as well as at the climb. The ridge is the side from which a neighbour arrives.

They live underground in the halls behind the stair-throat, so the exterior carries no dwellings of theirs. The taken labourers, twelve to fifteen, are housed in three mud shells of 30 m2. The other twenty-three structures are the works: courses, stairs, kiln, scaffolds, block face, hoist, gate and conduit.

It begins on the east side of the Hist court, from which the conduit head shows whole on the lip; from the foot of the face itself the rock hides it.
The lane along the pens, from the rack at the west end past the three doors to the head of the pens stair and the east pen; the labourers' one street.
The short worn line from the foot of the pens stair down to the terrace track, straight because it runs on the fall line between two stone pieces.

approaches.sequence: From the water south of the ring the nine trunks stand above the reeds like the teeth of a comb, the elder trunk tallest among them; as the boat noses to the pier the bank's mangroves take them one by one; from the pier head the southern gap and wall read together above the bank; the landing path climbs north-west to the arch.

approaches.wayfinding: Keep the tallest trunk ahead; the arch is the single gap in the wall. The path through it runs to the round house.

causalModel.founding: A village grown where nine root-joined trunks stand in one ring; one tree by the Hist's reckoning, nine by the tribes' reckoning.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A tribe that hosts the convocation's overflow and has grown rich on it, renting pitch-rights to delegations that cannot fit at the Tsoko camp.
causalModel.pressures: Hosting a province's delegations one month a year has made them arrogant the other eleven. Two neighbouring tribes now camp at Greenspring instead, on principle.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The ring of trunks encloses firm ground and makes its own stockade, with one gap left unbuilt for a gate. The knoll stands 4.8 m above the water table on firm lowland, with poleable water 32 m west and the Archon-Gideon road 160 m south-west.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A convocation held elsewhere would halve the village. The falling attendance the Root Talk ground counts publicly is already showing in their rents.

The arch and the ground either side of it: the single gap in the stockade, where a wary village turned hostile holds its line and through which a night raid comes.
The open pitch ground between the shelters and the spur, where the baggage of Under the Overflow is opened and a rent dispute in Pitch-Rights comes to blows.

causalModel.founding: The assembly designated this Hist for tapping and issued one licence against it: one stage, one season, one tree. The stage stands where the crew could raise it without cutting into the root flare.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A tapper and two crew whose licence is their livelihood. They keep the stage correct and police poachers themselves, because a district that cannot police itself loses its licences.
causalModel.pressures: The licence is renewed annually and the objection comes most reliably from the tribe whose tree carried the stage last year. Night landings at the same channel are not the crew's work; the crew do not stop them either.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: A firm terrace 3.1 m above the water table, 16 m from a channel deep enough (0.9 m) to pole a loaded canoe, under closed canopy that hides the camp from the land side until the last thirty metres.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A licence revoked would empty the stage within a season and make the same channel a poacher's road.

approaches.notes: The road arrives from the west-north-west; the city calls it the north gate because the road is the road north to Blackrose. The last 200 m bend twice, round the pond and over the shoulder.
approaches.sequence: From the road on the flat west of the pond the crown of the Hist shows over the trees on the crest, 40 m above the traveller. The road bends round the pond and the gate tower and the standing curtain hide the tree; the arch and the tower are what is seen. The road runs straight through the arch into the gate yard, holding its own bearing; the track then climbs the shoulder and the tree comes back on the left hand behind its ring of poles; at the top of the shoulder the bell kiosk shows ahead and the bay opens beyond it.

causalModel.founding: Rebuilt after the Slaughter of 4E 48 on the best natural harbour of the south coast, smaller and lower than the city it replaced.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: A reconstituted merchant council governs by tariff; it will not appoint a ruler. The last party that had one killed the city.
causalModel.pressures: Hostile to the An-Xileel successor state and indispensable to a bay that must trade somewhere. It is also built over its own mass grave.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: A firm crest above a shallow shelf: the stilt quarters step down from the crest to a tidal flat and a lighter quay. Big hulls anchor out on the 10 m plateau and their cargo comes ashore by lighter. The lightering is the city’s living.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: If the third Hist ever spoke to one faction alone, every institution here would break at once. The rules forbid it.

Pusbottom Remembers and the vault heist can turn to a fight in the lanes; the two-metre planks between huts are the tight class.

The Blackrose road runs in along the pond's north shore and reaches the bluff foot here, on the firm ground between the pond and the tidal flat; the city walls its gate across that line, so the road and the gate yard inside are one street.
The Archon lane leaves from the berth at which it arrives. A boat bound north is loaded at the quay off the pier, so the lane starts at the pier head. The city built no second landing.

The Blackrose lane comes down out of the marsh from the north-west and joins the same channel head. Poled craft come alongside the quay from the landward side of the berth, so one quay serves all three lanes.

The Soulrest lane comes up the estuary from the west and can go no further than the channel head. The shelf inside is too shallow for a laden hull, so the run ends at the lighter quay and the pier carries the cargo up to the deck.
The tender mooring is the sea-side end of the city. The dredged channel runs from the pier head out to it; no hull comes further in than its piles.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: settlement-register.md §2 (M5, rebuilt smaller); lilmoth.md owner decision 2026-08-24 (smaller, lower, over a mass grave); 95-build-sequence.md (M5 quest band 35–60); Morrowind:Balmora as the ratio check at about 40 buildings.
scaleGrounding.why: Twenty-six households in bamboo huts and the tall block, at five to a household, give about 130 residents; the council, the patrol, the tenders, the licence and salvage staff and the lighter crews housed on the quay add 60 to 100 more. Fifty-three placed structures is a third more than Balmora’s forty, which is the right size for a major city rebuilt smaller than the one that it replaced. Seventy named residents follows Morrowind’s ratio of named people to buildings.

candidates.why: The east face of the promontory. Section from the crest out: 21.9 m at 3640/6350, a 22.5° bluff, a 7.4 m bench at 3720/6350 (slope 2.5°), a tidal flat at 1.3–1.5 m from 3800 to 3860 (flood band 1–3, wet-season inundated), then 1.0 m of water at 3880, 3.8 m at 3920 and a 6.6 m roadstead plateau from 3960 to 4040. That is four buildable tiers and a drowned quarter in one 400 m run. The shallow shelf is 120 m wide, which is why large hulls anchor out and their cargo comes ashore by lighter (Lore:Lilmoth). 55 m from the approved anchor, well inside its 0.04 UV (296 m) tolerance.

candidates.rejectedBecause: The south-east embayment reaches 3.8 m of water 50 m off the shore and 15.5 m at 150 m. Deep water that close means a hull could berth alongside, which contradicts the record in Lore:Lilmoth that the city is built over shallow water and lighters its cargo. It also has no bench between the shore and the crest, so the city would be one tier, not three.
candidates.why: Shore at roughly 3790/6540, water 0.6 m at 3798/6548, 3.8 m at 3826/6576, 9.6 m at 3855/6605, 25.5 m at 3939/6689; the SE ray falls 18.6 m to the waterline over 280 m with no flat step.

candidates.rejectedBecause: The southern lagoon behind the spit is 0.4–0.6 m deep at 3600/6590–6630 and land again at 3600/6670. Nothing there can be drowned to dive depth, so the drowned quarter, the record's signature, would be a puddle. No lighter could reach open water.
candidates.why: Sheltered water and a natural breakwater, which is why it was measured at all: 2.0 m of land at 3600/6510, 1.05 m at 3600/6550, 0.4 m of water at 3600/6590, land at 1.6 m again at 3600/6670.

ways.why: The council walkway, the one surveyed line in the Argonian city, laid straight along the bench from the spine track to the bell.
The plank landing off the council walkway to the hall's own front, so the sitting is entered from the walkway and not off the bench grass.
The short pier from the divers’ shed to the diving stair.
The lighter pier from the quay deck east to the head of the channel, where the lighters come alongside.
The short landing that carries the loop's west lane to the rooming house's door, because the tenants come home in the dark and the bluff foot is mud.
The cross lane, a skewed plank link from the west lane to the east lane across the middle of the quarter, so a hut on the far side is reached without walking the whole loop.

The loop walkway of Pusbottom: a west lane that follows the bluff foot and bends with it, a short south lane over the wet ground and an east lane on piles over the shallows back up to the quay deck. Planks run straight from pile to pile between its bends, so no leg of it is a ruled line. None of it is a worn path.
The quay lane along the water’s edge from the lantern at the stair foot past the licence house and the lamp to the deck.
The boardwalk from the south corner of Pusbottom, clear of the corner hut, over the wet flat to the fishers’ row and the boat awning.
The spine across the north of Pusbottom from the stair foot to the quay deck, the busiest planks in the city.
The dredged navigation line from the pier head to the roadstead, the one water deep enough for a laden lighter across the shelf.

approaches.notes: The overland approach for anyone crossing the rootland from the north or west. The knoll is the ground from which the lair is surveyed before it is entered; the descent to the bank passes the cave mouth, so the swim entrance is found during the descent rather than sought.
approaches.sequence: From the rise to the west the bare scarred crown of the north dead tree stands 8 m above the live canopy; the live trees between the rise and the knoll then hide the water as the ground climbs to 12 m; the stand's ramp comes into view head-on on the knoll top; from the deck the whole pan, the cairns, the platform and the cave mouth are seen at once; the stand path then drops past the dead willow and the cave mouth to the offering shelf.
approaches.wayfinding: Walk east toward the bare crown; the ramp of the stand faces the walker on the knoll top. The path round the banks leaves from its foot.

approaches.fromDirection: south-east, up the creek from the estuary, following the pole line
approaches.notes: The survey has no water north of the pond, so the lane is approached from the estuary to the south-east rather than from the north; the poles run 180 m and the walk from the landing is 150 m with a climb of 8 m. Under this canopy the first-seen object is the first cue on the way, a pole, because no beacon can reach a boat on a 6 m creek.
approaches.sequence: The mouth pole shows first where the creek leaves the estuary; the poles then lead up the creek under a canopy of 0.93 while the water narrows to a boat's width and the pond stays out of sight; the head pole and the landing end the water; the bank path climbs west with the pond still hidden behind the slope; at the last bend the sky hole opens, the two dead cypresses show against it and then the water, with the lantern and the platform on its south shelf.
approaches.wayfinding: Follow the poles up the creek to the landing, then the trodden path uphill toward the bare crowns; the offering bank is where the path meets the water again.

causalModel.founding: An adult wamasu grew into a small perched pan of standing water west of the zone's poling creeks and has held it for years.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: The animal holds ground that it can charge; the villages have stopped trying to take it back and leave offerings on the south bank in the old Shadowfen manner.
causalModel.pressures: Boats keep to the pole-marked creek below the pond rather than the shorter line past it; the detour costs two hours and the pole line needs patching every season.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The one closed body of still water within 300 m: fed by the water table, cut off from the tidal creeks, some ten metres above the creek that carries them and shallow enough that the animal can stand in all of it. A low bank ring, a knoll above the north-west shore and a cave mouth at the west waterline that floods to the roof.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: Killing the animal reopens the direct line and ends the offerings; the tribes disagree about whether that is a gain.

combatSpaces.why: The retreat ground for the pond fight: the offering shelf, the chime and the cairn steps are deliberately cluttered, so that they are worse ground for the animal's charge and better ground for a fighter's retreat.

The lair is the fight: the adult wamasu holds the pan and charges anything that enters it, so the water and its rim are kept clear of everything but the three dead trees. The animal is the armoured daedroth build on the werewolfbeast rig with a body of roughly 5 m, which needs room to turn, charge and be circled; LN05 and the province hostility system both put the boss fight here.

scaleGrounding.why: A beast lair is sized by its creature count and its structure count, not by households: the adult variant of the recipe carries a single resident animal. Its two structures are the abandoned hunter's stand named in the recipe and the offering platform that Lore:Haynekhtnamet licenses. No dwelling, no door, no resident people. The count is two. The stand's footing and its deck are one structure in two stacked pieces, so the validator counts the structure and not its parts.
